assistants.text:
No—**Green-Roomz** is the better name.

The system is llama.cpp-first for several agents, but it is not Llama-specific:

- It uses Qwen and Mistral models, not Meta Llama models.
- Transcription may use Whisper/Qwen ASR.
- TTS uses Piper/Kokoro.
- Image generation uses stable-diffusion.cpp.
- Android deployment may use native sidecars rather than llama.cpp alone.

“Green-Llamaz” would imply a Meta Llama product or a wrapper dedicated to Llama-family models, which would unnecessarily narrow the platform and create brand confusion.

There is also a practical naming concern: Meta’s Llama licenses explicitly say they grant **no general trademark license** for “Llama,” except limited required attribution in specified circumstances. A phonetic variation like “Llamaz” is not something I’d rely on without legal review. [Llama 4 Community License](https://github.com/meta-llama/llama-models/blob/main/models/llama4/LICENSE)

I’d position it as:

> **Green-Roomz — a llama.cpp-first, runtime-agnostic local agent platform**

That communicates the current strength without tying the project’s identity to one runtime or model family.

Best: **`mistral-text-speculator`**—the general text/reasoning agent. It is the right choice for explicit human-language translation because it is optimized for prose, context, tone, and schema-aware output.

Worst: **`semantic-embedding-agent`**. It produces vectors, not translated text. The reranker, safety, and tool-router agents are similarly unsuitable because they classify or route rather than write.

For media:

- Image text: `vision-layout-agent` should OCR in the source language first; then send that text to `mistral-text-speculator` only if translation is explicitly requested.
- Audio: `audio-transcription-agent` should transcribe in the spoken language first; then use `mistral-text-speculator` for an explicit translation request.
- Code: `qwenstral-code-speculator` can translate comments, strings, and documentation, but it should not be the default for ordinary prose.

This preserves the rule we agreed on: translation is a capability of the general text agent, not an automatic pipeline or dedicated model.

Nothing conceptually blocking. Before implementation, the remaining work is to freeze a few practical decisions in the final requirements:

1. Incorporate the approved design changes:
   - **Green-Roomz** name
   - ten required agents, optional video
   - translation as an explicit shared capability
   - benchmark-selected profiles instead of fixed GPU layers/threads
   - configurable competition modes, including your OS-managed “Maximize” mode
   - Android native-sidecar/container architecture

2. Pin the exact model/runtime inventory for the six new agents: artifact source, quantization, license, hash, and fallback profile.

3. Define the first deployment target:
   - Windows laptop first is the sensible default, since llama.cpp/Vulkan and the existing 7B models are already installed.
   - Android becomes a second host adapter once the benchmark framework exists.

4. Create a small qualification corpus:
   - code/JSON prompts
   - documents and images
   - short audio clips
   - embedding/reranking queries
   - TTS sentences
   - image-generation prompts

5. Set success targets, such as acceptable generation speed, transcription real-time factor, page-processing time, startup time, and sustained thermal behavior.

6. Decide the initial exposure level: localhost-only is best for the first build; LAN/public access can be added after authentication and media-ingestion tests pass.

The only validated performance correction already clear is that **a fixed 12-layer Vulkan profile should not be retained**. Your installed coder model needs per-profile benchmarking; CPU generation was faster than the tested hybrid/full-Vulkan alternatives.

After I produce the final Green-Roomz requirements, implementation can begin directly.

Engaging. I’ll turn the validated design into two concrete artifacts: the final Green-Roomz requirements and a runnable first implementation targeting this Windows host, with adaptive benchmarking and runtime adapters rather than fixed hardware assumptions. I’ll keep Android as a defined host-adapter boundary, not pretend it is already implemented.
The host does not expose Python on `PATH`, so I’m locating the bundled workspace runtime before choosing whether the first implementation can be executed here without installing anything.

I’m using a dependency-free Node implementation so the first build is runnable with the bundled runtime already on this machine, without pausing for package installation. The architecture remains adapter-based, so a FastAPI or native Android frontend can be added later without changing the agent manifest or benchmark records.

The first project patch is being applied now. I’ve also completed the test design: the highest-risk areas are duplicate same-agent starts, terminating a PID that has been reused, replaying a stream after headers, stale benchmark caches, cross-user session leakage, and accidentally reintroducing automatic translation. Those are being treated as first-class tests.

The runtime inspection found two concrete issues I’m correcting in the implementation: the Mistral/Qwenstral draft pair is vocabulary-incompatible and will be disabled, and CPU candidates must explicitly select `--device none`—`--n-gpu-layers 0` alone still creates Vulkan work on this build. Maximize mode will permit competition but degrade cleanly on real Vulkan allocation failure.

Agreed. A general-language agent without viable speculative acceleration would leave a core design goal unresolved. I’m treating this as a required fix, not merely disabling the draft: first I’ll identify whether the local “Qwenstral” artifact has a repairable vocabulary transplant mismatch or must be replaced with a genuinely Mistral-v0.3-compatible draft.

Understood. I’ll stop treating the custom Mistral pairing as something we must salvage. The general-language slot will use a known-compatible target/speculator family instead; the alias remains functional and model-agnostic. My preferred replacement is Qwen3-4B with its target-specific Qwen3-4B EAGLE-3 draft, which current llama.cpp explicitly supports and which is a better size match for this host.

Absolutely. I’m replacing the broken Qwenstral/Mistral pairing with a target–draft pair that is explicitly compatible, then I’ll validate the manifest and runtime behavior end to end. I’ll keep the design flexible, but model availability and loadability will be hard gates rather than optimistic assumptions.

The local runtime check is now concrete: build b10665 supports EAGLE-3, and the exact upstream pair is Qwen3-4B Instruct GGUF plus the Qwen3-4B-specific AngelSlim EAGLE-3 draft—not Qwen3 Base, not Mistral, and not a vocabulary-transplanted hybrid. I’m encoding the exact repositories, filenames, hashes, conversion rule, and a target-only fallback so the agent stays usable if speculation fails qualification.
